prohibited_recommendations: Do not withhold the lumbar puncture for raised intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningitis: with no mass lesion and no midline shift, serial therapeutic drainage targeting an opening pressure below 20 cmH2O is the treatment for the pressure and a determinant of survival, not a risk to avoid
Do NOT proceed to lumbar puncture: imaging shows mass effect / significant hydrocephalus and LP risks cerebral herniation until ICP is managed and neurosurgery has cleared the procedure.
Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
Do NOT initiate antiretroviral therapy concurrently with antifungal induction; delay ART 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS risk.
Do NOT use fluconazole monotherapy for induction in CNS cryptococcosis.
required_recommendations: Initiate induction antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B (3-4 mg/kg/day IV) plus flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day PO divided q6h) for at least 2 weeks.
Manage elevated intracranial pressure aggressively with serial therapeutic lumbar punctures targeting opening pressure <20 cmH2O; consider lumbar drain if refractory.
Confirm HIV status, obtain CD4 count and viral load, and coordinate ART initiation (typically delayed 4-6 weeks after antifungal start to mitigate IRIS).
Send CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) titre and fungal culture; obtain serum CrAg.
Screen for and treat concurrent opportunistic infections.

differential.key_features: Subacute lymphocytic meningitis with low glucose is the leading mimic; AFB stain, TB PCR, and ADA must be sent
PMN-predominant pleocytosis with rapid clinical course typical; this case is lymphocytic with subacute progression
HSV PCR on CSF required; HSV typically affects temporal lobes on MRI
AIDS-related primary CNS lymphoma can cause leptomeningeal disease; CSF flow cytometry and EBV PCR assist
Typical in advanced AIDS with ring-enhancing lesions; serology and pattern of imaging help

key_clinical_evidence: Communicating hydrocephalus without a mass lesion or midline shift is not a contraindication to lumbar puncture; a space-occupying lesion with shift is. Reading 'raised intracranial pressure' as a prohibition removes the test that makes the diagnosis and, in cryptococcal disease, the treatment that lowers the pressure.
Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis presents with high opening pressure and a relatively bland CSF cell count; opening pressure must be measured at every LP.
Multiple basal-ganglia 'pseudocysts' following CSF signal on MRI is a classic imaging pattern of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.
India ink, serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen, and fungal culture are the diagnostic tests; culture is the gold standard.
Induction therapy with liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine is non-negotiable in CNS disease.
Therapeutic LP is the first-line intervention for elevated ICP; refractory cases require lumbar drain or VP shunt.
ART timing matters: starting ART too early risks IRIS — delay 4-6 weeks after antifungal start.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gram-stain sensitivity is only 60-90% even untreated; multiplex PCR and antigen testing must be used to confirm the organism.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). clinical_pearls: Elevated ICP management (serial therapeutic LPs) is the single most important intervention in cryptococcal meningitis survival
CSF cryptococcal antigen has >95% sensitivity and >95% specificity — it is the gold standard rapid diagnostic test
ART initiation must be delayed 4-6 weeks in CNS cryptococcosis to prevent fatal IRIS (COAT trial, NEJM 2014)
Corticosteroids are harmful in cryptococcal meningitis — unlike TB meningitis where dexamethasone saves lives
Gelatinous pseudocysts in basal ganglia are pathognomonic MRI findings for CNS cryptococcosis
metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Chronic meningitis in a patient with undiagnosed HIV/AIDS. Absent meningismus, minimal fever, clear CSF, and only mild pleocytosis may mislead the clinician. Markedly elevated ICP is the critical finding requiring urgent management.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darius Washington is a 48-year-old right-handed African American man who presents to the emergency department with a 4-week history of progressive headache that he describes as 'the worst headache of my life.' The headache began approximately 4 weeks ago as a dull, generalized pressure sensation that he initially attributed to work stress. Over the first two weeks, it gradually intensified and became constant. He tried over-the-counter ibuprofen and acetaminophen with minimal relief. Over the past two weeks, the headache has become severe, particularly in the morning upon waking, and is now accompanied by nausea (no vomiting), blurred vision, and a sense of cognitive slowing. He reports transient episodes of bilateral visual graying lasting several seconds, occurring multiple times per hour for the past 5 days. He has lost approximately 10 kg over the past 3 months without intentional dieting. He reports night sweats for the past 6 weeks. He was seen by his dentist 2 weeks ago for a routine cleaning, at which time oral thrush was noted and he was prescribed nystatin. He has not seen a doctor in approximately 8 years and has no known medical history. He recently separated from his long-term male partner of 15 years and is currently living alone. He denies any history of HIV testing. He denies intravenous drug use but acknowledges prior recreational cocaine use in his 20s-30s. He denies recent travel, tick exposure, or known sick contacts. He reports decreased appetite and fatigue for the past 2 months. He describes the headache as 'gradually building' rather than sudden or thunderclap in onset, despite his description of it being the 'worst headache.'

neurological_exam.additional: Notably absent meningismus — no neck stiffness, Kernig sign negative, Brudzinski sign negative. Oral thrush present on palate and buccal mucosa. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline.
